title: Couldn't type shift with Powertoys open

judgment.rationale: The new commenter supplied a useful constrained reproduction: Shift fails system-wide, including the on-screen keyboard, while raw low-level events still arrive and quitting PowerToys restores behavior. This is enough for maintainer-side hook isolation, but not enough to assign a root cause or call the older duplicate classification valid.
evidence: The original report says Shift stopped working with Keyboard Manager turned off and PowerToys had to be stopped to restore it.
A 2026-10-21 commenter reproduced system-wide loss on PowerToys 0.100.0 / Windows 11 25H2, with no remaps configured in Keyboard Manager.
That commenter reports that a low-level keyboard logger still received balanced raw Shift and slash events, that alternative remappers did not restore the symptom, and that quitting PowerToys did.
The commenter lists the active PowerToys modules and states the issue occurred without using PowerToys features.
judgment.recommended_action: Reproduce with the reported module set and instrument which active PowerToys hook consumes the event before proposing a module-specific fix.

fix_assessment.rationale: The repository has a shared low-level KeyboardHook that returns a handled result after an active callback, making hook-consumption behavior a testable hypothesis. No evidence yet identifies which callback is responsible or confirms a defect in that implementation.

proposed_fixes.title: Preserve Shift events unless an active module intentionally consumes them
proposed_fixes.root_cause: An active global keyboard callback may be returning a consumed result for an unrelated Shift event even when Keyboard Manager has no remaps; the exact module and callback are not identified.
plan: Replay the reported Shift-loss scenario while tracing low-level hook registration order, module callback activity, and each callback's handled result.
Identify the first callback that consumes Shift when its feature should not own that event.
Narrow the callback predicate or pass the unrelated event through, and add a test for Shift down/up with that feature enabled but inactive.
verification: Confirm Shift works in ordinary applications and the on-screen keyboard with the reported module set.
Verify any intentionally registered Shift-based shortcut still works and that no key-down/key-up pair is lost.

confidence.rationale: The raw-event and PowerToys-shutdown comparisons implicate a PowerToys hook chain, but do not identify which active callback handles the event.

issue_context.summary: A recent confirmation narrows the intermittent Shift loss to a PowerToys-running condition despite Keyboard Manager being disabled and no remaps configured.
known_information: The original reporter used PowerToys 0.90.1 and had Keyboard Manager off.
A second reporter observed the issue on PowerToys 0.100.0 / Windows 11 25H2 with Keyboard Manager enabled but an empty remap configuration.
The second reporter says the on-screen keyboard was affected, raw low-level Shift events arrived in order, and quitting PowerToys restored Shift.
The second reporter says disabling Sticky/Filter Keys and quitting several other key utilities one at a time did not restore Shift.
inferences: A PowerToys low-level hook may consume an event further down the chain, but the module and exact transition are unknown.
The original and second report may share an owner, but the original report alone does not establish the same machine state or trigger.
issue_context.analysis: The new report is more specific than the original artifact's unsupported duplicate/handled classification. The correct next discriminator is a maintainer-side trace of active hook callbacks, not a generic request for more logs from a reporter who already supplied key-event evidence.
initial_investigation: Read the complete issue body and its one full comment, including the module list and key-event observations.

Read KeyboardHook::HookProc in src/common/interop/KeyboardHook.cpp: it iterates active callbacks and returns 1 when a callback handles an event; this is a possible ownership boundary, not proof of the failing callback.
No public linked PR or explicit duplicate is present in the issue discussion.

actions.label: Trace the Shift event consumer
actions.note: Do not start a module-specific implementation design until the consuming callback is identified.

actions.label: Trace Shift with the reported modules

reproduce.title: Isolate the PowerToys callback that consumes Shift
reproduce.version_requirement: Current stable build, then 0.100.0 only if needed to compare with the confirmation
prerequisites: Windows 11 25H2-class system with a standard keyboard layout.
Keyboard Manager enabled with no remaps; match the reporter's available module set where practical.
Instrumentation that records hook callback entry/return for Shift without recording typed content.
steps: Start PowerToys with the matched module set and verify Shift works in a text editor and the on-screen keyboard.
Leave PowerToys running without invoking module UI or shortcuts; periodically test Shift in the same applications.
If Shift stops working, capture callback return decisions while pressing and releasing Shift and a shifted punctuation key.
Disable one PowerToys module at a time only after recording the failing trace, then compare against a fully stopped PowerToys run.
reproduce.expected_result: Shift down/up reaches the target and on-screen keyboard consistently; if a callback consumes it, the trace names the exact callback and state that justified consumption.
